AI and Chip Stocks Race Ahead
 
Plus, Paramount settles and crude prices drop again
 
By Heard on the Street Staff
 
 
DANIEL COLE/REUTERS
 

This is an edition of the Markets P.M. newsletter, a recap of the day’s most important markets moves, delivered after the closing bell. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here.

 
 
 

What Happened in Markets Today

 

A rally in tech stocks led stocks to a strong start to the week. Tech giants including Intel and Meta Platforms surged on Monday, as investors piled into bets on chips and AI hyperscalers. The Nasdaq Composite index gained 2.3%, its best session since early August. The S&P 500 added 1.5%, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average added 366 points, or 0.7%.

 

Oil extended a stretch of declines. Brent crude futures fell 3.5%, or by about $3.50 a barrel, to just over $100 on Monday. It was the biggest one-day decline since August, and extended its steak of declines to four sessions, the longest since June. Investors will be looking to see whether President Trump meets with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian at the U.N. gathering beginning this week.

 

A Hollywood-shaking deal is cleared to proceed. Paramount reached a settlement with states that had brought antitrust concerns, clearing the way for its hard-fought $81 billion merger with Warner Bros. Discovery. Warner shares surged nearly 11%, and Paramount fell almost 3%.

 

Meta’s new AI agent is fueling optimism. The recent release of the agent, Muse, has sparked a fire under Meta’s shares. One analyst on Monday outlined a scenario in which Muse could add over $28 billion in additional revenue for the company by 2030. Meta shares jumped over 11% on Monday.

 

Bitcoin didn’t get the crypto winter memo. Although shares of crypto companies tumbled hard after the Clarity Act failed to clear a legislative hurdle last week, bitcoin’s price moved above $86,000 for the first time since January. Coinbase Global and Circle Internet Group also rallied, rising about 3.5% and 3%, respectively.

One Big Story

 
 
SHANNON STAPLETON/REUTERS
 

Uranium enrichment—a key step in making nuclear fuel—is a unique corner of the energy market. Only two companies, both in Europe, hold enrichment capacity outside Russia and China. American company Centrus Energy is hoping to disrupt that world order.

 

Centrus shares rode an AI wave over the past few years, peaking late last year. Since then, its shares have lost steam alongside other nuclear stocks. It is down 67% from its peak. But it looks less speculative than some nuclear plays.
